#4390. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson said the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a big truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

#4389. BYD Is Winning Over Japan With A Very Japanese Kind Of EV

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BYD’s latest milestone in Japan would barely register on its sales charts back home in China. But selling 10,000 cars in a country dominated by domestic brands is progress, especially when part of that momentum comes from selling a vehicle tailored to what Japanese buyers actually want: a small, practical box on wheels, which also happens to be electric.

The Chinese automaker announced that its cumulative Japanese passenger-car sales had passed 10,000. Its first 5,000 took roughly two and a half years after deliveries began in January 2023. The next 5,000 took about 15 months. That includes its entire lineup, rather than just its newest and arguably most interesting addition: the Racco electric kei car.

It was bold to challenge Japan’s homegrown manufacturers with something designed specifically for their market and to create the world’s first kei car from a non-Japanese automaker. The Racco’s tall body, tiny footprint, and sliding rear doors follow the familiar Japanese formula for such vehicles. BYD didn’t need to reinvent anything, but its entry needed to be convincing.

Japanese buyers’ initial response to the Racco was encouraging. Launched on July 28, it attracted 1,002 orders in two weeks, the fastest order intake of any BYD model in Japan. By the end of August, that had grown to around 1,500. Roughly 80% of buyers chose the range-topping 300 Premium, clearly showing that the cheapest version was less attractive.

BYD credited the Racco with helping deliver record monthly orders across its Japanese lineup in August. Potential buyers who came to see the little EV ended up discovering its other models, too.

BYD offers six passenger-car models in Japan, and every one has a charging port. Five are fully electric: the Racco kei car, Dolphin hatchback, Seal sedan, Atto 3 crossover, and Sealion 7 SUV. The sixth, the Sealion 6 SUV, is a plug-in hybrid combining a gasoline engine with electric propulsion. That makes the entire lineup electrified, with no gasoline-only cars or conventional, non-plug-in hybrids on offer.

What’s more interesting is comparing the Racco’s sales performance to its main rival, the Nissan Sakura EV, which is also Japan’s best-selling electric car. In October, the Sakura EV sold 878 units, while the Racco sold 607. That’s almost 70% of the volume, marking a 37% rise over September.

The Nissan Sakura EV was Japan’s electric bestseller for a fourth consecutive year in 2025, but it could lose its crown to the Racco, which gives buyers more battery for less money, at least before subsidies. It starts at ¥2.145 million with a 22.4-kWh pack and 130 miles (210 kilometers) of WLTC range, while the Sakura starts at ¥2.449 million with a 20-kWh battery and 112 miles (180 km).

Even the longer-range Racco, with a 35.8-kWh pack capable of 199 miles (320 km), undercuts the entry-level Nissan at ¥2.398 million. The BYD also gets sliding rear doors instead of the Nissan’s conventional ones. What could help the Sakura stay ahead is the larger government subsidy it benefits from, which can make it cheaper to buy despite its higher sticker price.

It’s a tad early to call the Racco a Japanese sensation, but buyers are clearly interested. This newcomer is already selling roughly seven cars for every ten Sakuras in one month, so it definitely deserves attention.

#4388. AO3 is Back Online After Two Long Weeks Without Clerith Fanfics

The internet has spent the past two and a half weeks deprived of many important things, including easy access to stories in which Cloud Strife and Aerith Gainsborough get the ending their readers wanted. Fortunately for Clerith fans, Archive of Our Own (AO3) is finally back online.

The volunteer-run fanfiction archive returned on Sunday, November 15, after going offline on October 29. Its operator, the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), says a security incident prompted the extended shutdown. AO3 is usable again, although it hasn’t quite returned to normal.

This is a detailed explanation about the limitations of Phoenix Down in Final Fantasy 7.

For anyone who hasn’t spent much time on AO3, it’s a huge collection of fan-written stories covering games, movies, books, television, and just about any other fictional universe you can name.

Some stories fill gaps in the original work; others toss canon aside altogether. In Final Fantasy 7’s case, the apparently immortal debate about Cloud’s love life is practically built for it. Even Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth director Naoki Hamaguchi refuses to settle the Aerith-or-Tifa question.

OTW says it was able to reopen the archive before the far end of its four-week recovery estimate by switching off a handful of features. User and collection icons currently don’t appear, importing works from other websites is unavailable, and the only download option is HTML. No icons were deleted; they just aren’t being shown yet.

Traffic is another problem. AO3 has warned that some users will see slow loading times or even the maintenance page as it manages demand. Refreshing and trying again is the recommendation, although it may take a little patience to get in.

Initially, the October 29 outage looked like ordinary maintenance. The situation changed when OTW disclosed evidence of a security incident and warned that recovery could take between two and four weeks. It has brought in a security firm to review the incident, but isn’t detailing its fixes while that work is underway.

The return also comes just after AO3’s seventeenth anniversary. Not a particularly fun way to celebrate, but at least readers can now get back to their bookmarks.

One of the bigger worries during the shutdown was what would happen to unfinished drafts. AO3 normally removes drafts after 30 days, which is a nasty surprise if you haven’t been able to log in for more than two weeks. OTW says it paused automatic deletion throughout the outage, and no drafts were lost.

That pause will remain in place until November 29. The catch is that dates shown on existing drafts may still reflect their original deadlines, not the extension. Writers are being asked to review unfinished work and save or publish it before automatic deletion resumes.

OTW also says published works, bookmarks, kudos, and other archive data remain intact. That’s the good news. The security side is less settled, though. The organization says it has no reason to think its user database was compromised, but it can’t be ruled out.

It recommends an AO3 password change, as well as on other sites if you’ve reused your AO3 credentials there. You can follow further updates on the official AO3 status page.

Look, you don’t need to have read a single fanfic to understand the appeal. Games ask you to spend dozens, sometimes hundreds, of hours with fictional people. Once the credits roll, it’s hardly surprising that some players want to spend more time with them, or imagine things going differently.

The Final Fantasy 7 fandom is an obvious example. We have covered how central Tifa and Aerith are to Rebirth’s story, while a separate guide to Aerith’s relationship options shows how much attention players can pay to Cloud’s relationships. The official story gives players scenes and choices to dissect. Fanfiction lets them carry the argument somewhere else, without waiting for Square Enix to settle anything.

Fanfiction lets them carry the argument somewhere else, without waiting for Square Enix to settle anything.

Beyond the romance, fans have been reimagining Final Fantasy 7’s cast in entirely different art styles for years. Writing an alternate ending or inventing a crossover isn’t so different in spirit. AO3 simply gives that kind of work a home, a tag system, and readers who actually go looking for it.

After 17 days of an error page, that home is accessible again. If you left a story half-read on October 28, there’s finally a chance to find your place. Just don’t be surprised if everyone else had the same idea

#4387. Tested: The 2026 Lexus ES Hybrid Evolves, but It Has a Familiar Feel

Larger than before and with a significantly revamped interior, the new ES350h nonetheless stays the course with its cushy driving demeanor.

11/12/26 UPDATE: This review has been updated with instrumented test results.

Although Lexus is no stranger to sporty models, this luxury brand made its name on quiet, plush sedans that prioritize refinement above all else. And the ES is the one that has persisted. This comfy cruiser was the bestselling Lexus for many years, and it continues to attract a loyal set of buyers. Understandably, Lexus has been reluctant to change the ES formula much throughout its seven generations thus far.

On the surface, that appears to change with the new eighth-generation Lexus ES. Not only does the ES look quite different inside and out for 2026, but it also offers an electric powertrain for the first time. The ES hybrid continues, however, and after driving the latest version, it’s clear that this sedan's core mission hasn't changed as much as you might think.

Lexus first offered the ES as a hybrid for 2013, and the previous-generation gas-electric model made up around 40 percent of ES sales last year. Given that take rate, it makes sense that the old nonhybrid V-6 has been axed. The electric ES, which we review separately, is a big departure for this model line, but Lexus expects the hybrid to make up 80 percent of ES sales in the U.S. So, for now at least, the EV will be a niche product, and the gas-electric model will be the volume seller.

See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 94043

With a longer wheelbase, a significantly taller profile, and a more imposing shape, the new ES stretches to the larger end of the mid-size luxury-sedan segment. Lexus engineers say they tried to “eliminate the negatives” of the sedan shape with this model, such as the more difficult ingress and egress of a lower seating height. In other words, it follows the tall-sedan format of the Toyota Crown but attempts to disguise its stature with more angular styling and a swoopy roofline that tapers toward the short trunk lid. There are some awkward angles, but overall, the design works and is still recognizable as a Lexus.

The ES hybrid gets the latest Toyota hybrid powertrain, which the company refers to as the sixth-generation setup. It has a different power unit and transmission than before, and it’s configured to prioritize the electric motors for propulsion more. The 2.5-liter gasoline four-cylinder engine doesn’t change much, but total combined output of 244 horsepower is up from the previous ES300h’s 215 horses. That’s apparently enough for Lexus to bump the badge up to ES350h. All-wheel drive is optional on the hybrid ES for the first time, courtesy of an additional electric motor on the rear axle, though it doesn’t change output figures compared with the front-wheel-drive configuration.

The all-wheel-drive ES350h we tested got to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, which is a significant improvement over the previous, front-wheel-drive ES300h F Sport’s 7.9-second run. That’s despite a significant weight gain, as our test car tipped the scales at 4145 pounds, 352 more than the 2023 ES300h we last tested.

See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 94043

While this four-cylinder powertrain isn’t quite as smooth or sonorous as the old nonhybrid ES350’s V-6, the upgraded gas-electric setup is appreciably more refined than the old hybrid was. The gas engine is well isolated from the cabin and only makes itself known under hard acceleration; the hushed 67 decibels and 21 sones of noise we recorded inside at 70 mph is perfectly acceptable here. The electric motors go about their business seamlessly, with imperceptible switching between gas and electric power, and while the embiggened ES doesn’t quite feel eager, it accelerates with sufficient gusto and generally is responsive to throttle inputs. EPA ratings sit at 46 mpg combined with front-wheel drive and 44 mpg with all-wheel drive—strong numbers for this large of a sedan. We averaged 37 mpg overall, and the ES matched its 42-mpg EPA highway estimate in our 75-mph real-world fuel-economy test. But that’s not quite as good as the previous model, a 2019 ES300h which managed 45 mpg in the same test.

Importantly, the ride quality is fantastic. The suspension is tuned to be soft, as you’d expect for a boulevardier like this, but we appreciate the nicely controlled body motions. And the all-season tires have plenty of sidewall for soaking up potholes and rough sections of road (relatively small 19-inch wheels are the only choice on the hybrid model for now). This isn’t a vehicle for hard cornering, and the eco-conscious rubber doesn’t provide much grip when you push it around corners, but the steering wheel feels good in your hands and provides satisfactory on-center feel and natural effort buildup. We recorded a ho-hum 0.84 g of grip around our skidpad and a 170-foot stop from 70 mph.

Upon first glance at the cabin, you might worry that Lexus has too eagerly adopted the button-free, touch-capacitive interiors that are becoming too commonplace. And while there are definitely fewer buttons and knobs than before, and more controls integrated into the large 14.0-inch touchscreen, Lexus has done a good job balancing function with form. There’s still a volume knob, for instance, and although most climate functions are now on a lower part of the screen, there are a few crucial tactile buttons for adjusting the temperature and turning on the defrosters. The steering-wheel controls look like they’re touch-sensitive, but they’re thankfully tactile too. And the secondary functions such as mirror controls, seat adjustments, and windows are all still conventional and intuitive.

The material finishes and build quality live up to Lexus’s high standard. But it is worth noting that the hybrid comes in Premium and Premium+ trims, which means it doesn’t offer some of the most high-end features and accoutrements of the electric model’s Luxury trim. Pricing for the ES350h ($51,095 to start) is up $6380 over the previous ES300h, but you do get more car—namely in the physical sense—and the ES still costs significantly less than a BMW 5-series or a Mercedes-Benz E-class. Our Premium-trim test car featured a few options and still came in at under $55,000.

Lexus is notoriously risk-averse with its most popular models, and ultimately the company’s conservatism has paid off with this new ES. It’s more modern-looking inside and out and offers more technology than before, but Lexus wisely didn’t make many changes to the core tenets that have made the ES a success. It still offers a comfortable ride and a cosseting interior, and these qualities combined with the hybrid powertrain’s quiet operation and impressive fuel efficiency should continue to please the ES faithful.

#4386. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD was going 74 mph before fiery crash that killed 3

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police said it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

@Fred Lambert I was going to ask if you're collecting all of these onto a page so people can find them all and I just found that your first link at the top points to the original article and you're updating that with links to all articles as I wanted. Thanks for that and now I have a place to send a friend who wants to buy a Tesla with FSD and thinks he'll never have to watch the road.

What stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

Tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A company that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

We’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

#4385. Scout’s New Truck and SUV Are Another Step Closer to Reality

The VW-owned company has started validation builds of the Terra and Traveler at its new $2 billion factory in Blythewood, South Carolina.

Just like vehicles themselves, automotive manufacturing plants have to go through a lot of testing before cranking out the first production model. Scout Motors broke ground on its Blythewood, South Carolina, plant about two and a half years ago, and as final bits of construction wrap up, the VW Group subsidiary is beginning to build validation vehicles to test production processes.

When Scout reemerged a few years ago to bring back the practical, can-do vehicles that defined the brand in the 1960s and ’70s, it aimed to build a fleet of hybrid and electric body-on-frame off-roaders that blended modern amenities with vintage charm. The automaker plans to launch a Terra pickup truck and a Traveler SUV for the 2028 model year.

See all results for new 2028 Scout Terra for sale near 94043

It looks like Scout is still on track to stick with that timeline. The automaker has announced that most of the manufacturing parts are already up and running, with validation vehicles beginning to make their way through the body, paint, and assembly shops. Validation vehicles are kind of like a practice run, giving employees the ability to problem-solve and refine processes without having to keep a tight schedule.

Alongside the new equipment, Scout is testing out more than 750 robots in the body shop. The AI-supported bots will be used to monitor about 5000 weld points per vehicle for quality assurance. At full capacity, the body shop will be able to process about 40 vehicles per hour.

The Terra pickup and Traveler SUV are both expected to start at under $60,000. Scout says the validation process will continue into 2027, followed by more refined pre-production vehicles and eventually the finalized production model. That’s right in line with what Scott Keogh, Scout’s CEO, told us last year, when he projected that the first vehicles would go on sale by the end of 2027. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2028.

#4384. 2027 McLaren W1

They say that lightning never strikes the same place twice, let alone thrice, but McLaren is channeling Zeus with its newest W1 flagship. As a descendant of the hallowed McLaren F1 and a direct successor to the brand's last 903-hp P1 halo car, the W1 assumes a throne previously occupied by hypercar royalty. And if you couldn’t guess by its wind-sculpted, carbon-fiber-laden exterior, the W1 has the spec sheet to back up its noble position.

Wielding a 9200-rpm twin-turbo V-8 paired with an axial-flux electric motor, the W1 delivers 1258 horsepower to the pavement via its rear wheels, making it the most powerful McLaren ever. Those ponies don’t have to contend with much mass, as a carbon-fiber tub and body help keep the W1's dry weight to a feathery 3084 pounds. Active aerodynamics, including a rear wing that extends rearward up to 11.8 inches, add massive downforce and enable maximum attack at the racetrack. The W1 is a worthy heir to its predecessors, the latest in a highly accomplished bloodline of supersonic, roadgoing weaponry.

Expert Tip: When it comes to seven-digit, Formula-1-inspired race cars for the road, options are predictably limited. The Aston Martin Valhalla is another example, brandishing a 1064-horsepower plug-in-hybrid powertrain and a chassis developed with help from the Aston Martin Aramco Formula 1 Team.

With the W1 debuting just last year, we don’t expect any changes for the 2027 model year.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

The W1 uses a plug-in hybrid powertrain comprised of McLaren's MHP-8 turbocharged V-8 engine working in unison with a radial-flux electric motor and an 8-speed transmission; it sends power to the rear wheels. The V-8 alone is good for 916 horsepower, and the electric motor 342 horsepower. Combined, that's 1258 ponies, the highest output of any McLaren.

The electric element includes a motorsport-derived E-module: a radial flux motor and integrated Motor Control Unit weighing just 44 pounds, similar to the type used in IndyCar racing. (McLaren participates in that series as well as F1.) The electric motor is mounted to the transmission and can spin up to 24,000 rpm. The E-module is powered by a battery of about 1.4 kWh, enclosed in a structural carbon-fiber box located low in the chassis to optimize the center of gravity. The battery maintains a minimum level of charge to crank the engine on vehicle start-up and to power the electric reversing function. McLaren quotes an electric-only driving range of about two miles and a charging time of 22 minutes to bring the battery to 80 percent.

According to McLaren, the W1 can hit 60 mph in just 2.7 seconds. More remarkably, accelerating from 0-124 mph requires just 5.8 seconds. The pedals, steering wheel, instrument binnacle, and attendant controls move to help the driver find a comfortable position. Interior space is enhanced by concave sections on the inside door panels.

The McLaren W1 includes a comprehensive warranty and maintenance schedule. Similar to McLarens equipped with the V-6 hybrid, the V-8-hybrid-equipped W1 follows a 12-month service interval schedule that reflects McLaren series production supercars rather than schedules of its track-focused cars.

#4383. 10 Best Boss Fights in Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

Alongside its completely revamped visuals and modernized gameplay designed around the Joy-Cons, one of the things I was most excited about when I finally got my hands on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake was facing its bosses all over again.

I've played the original countless times, and there are so many incredible boss fights throughout this adventure that the mere thought of experiencing them again with all these changes was almost too exciting to handle. Thankfully, despite my ridiculously high expectations, it managed to exceed them. Congratulations, Nintendo, all my childhood nightmares have officially been upgraded!

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

Jokes aside, the remake does an incredible job of staying faithful to the original bosses while giving them enough visual and gameplay improvements to make these encounters feel fresh. And honestly, the excitement I felt when entering these arenas was just as strong as it was the first time around. And picking a favorite Ocarina of Time boss is still as difficult as picking just one Zelda game to call your favorite: there are simply too many amazing ones to choose from!

So, I decided to put together a ranking of the ten best boss fights in the new Ocarina of Time, including a few mini-bosses to make things even more interesting. Let's see which encounters managed to steal the spotlight. Naturally, there are lots of spoilers here if you haven't completed the remake or the original, so beware!

Fighting Gohma is actually pretty easy, I must say, but there's no denying that she makes a fantastic first impression as Ocarina of Time's opening boss. This is basically the first real test of your skills, giving you a taste of what's waiting for you throughout the rest of the adventure – and there's something incredibly satisfying about finally defeating your first major enemy.

Besides, her introduction is absolutely fantastic! You enter what appears to be an empty room, already anticipating the boss encounter because you know something is waiting for you. But there's nothing there. So, naturally, you look up... and surprise! Gohma is crawling across the ceiling, ready to ruin your day.

Her imposing size makes the encounter even more memorable, especially when you realize she's trying to give birth to a bunch of smaller spiders just to make your life miserable. Lovely! The remake takes all these elements and makes them even more impressive with its updated visuals, giving Gohma a much more intimidating presence. Not bad for our first big fight.

What's not to love about fighting a giant blob of goo? I'll admit that I never found Morpha particularly exciting in the original game, but the remake completely changed my mind.

One of my favorite things about this encounter is how quickly it goes from zero to one hundred. After surviving the Water Temple, you're probably expecting some terrifying aquatic monster, perhaps a giant shark or a creature covered in tentacles. Instead, you walk into the boss arena and find... a blob.

However, things get considerably more interesting once the battle begins. Morpha uses its gelatinous body to create enormous tentacles that can grab Link and take a surprisingly painful chunk out of his health. And believe me, they're considerably faster this time around, so you'll want to keep moving.

Falling into the water is also something you should avoid at all costs, since the rest of Morpha's body is lurking beneath the surface. It's a surprisingly stressful encounter, but also fun, especially because you have to use the Hookshot to pull Morpha's inner nucleus out of its tentacles and attack it. It's the only boss that requires you to use what is the coolest equipment in the game!

My first encounter with the Iron Knuckle in the remake was just as terrifying as I remembered it being in the original. This heavily armored enemy hits like a truck, and every successful attack can take a ridiculous amount of Link's health away. Even worse, its powerful strikes can send you flying across the arena, making it incredibly difficult to regain control of the situation.

A big part of what makes this encounter so intimidating is that you're facing the Iron Knuckle as Child Link. You're considerably weaker than Adult Link, and you don't have access to the powerful equipment and abilities you've grown accustomed to using throughout your adventure. So suddenly, you're reminded that you're still a pretty vulnerable little kid, and this walking tank is more than happy to prove it!

The remake's improved visuals make the encounter even more impressive, giving the Iron Knuckle an intimidating presence that makes every swing of its enormous axe feel dangerous. It's a little like eating your grandmother's homemade food after worrying that something might have gone wrong with the recipe. Somehow, it turns out even better than you remembered.

King Dodongo is an enormous creature that spends most of the fight rolling around its circular arena, trying to crush Link before eventually opening its mouth to unleash a fiery attack. What I love most about this boss is how clever its main weakness is. Since the creature seems so eager to swallow Link, let’s give it something else to eat, of course!

So all you need to do is avoid its rolling attacks and throw a Bomb into its mouth whenever it opens it, and watching this enormous beast swallow an explosive and immediately regret its life choices never gets old.

It's also a fantastic early boss because it makes you realize just how much bigger and more dangerous Hyrule is compared to the relatively cozy Kokiri Forest. Nothing says “your adventure is officially getting more challenging” quite like fighting a creature thirty times your size over a pool of lava.

Dead Hand has always been one of the most nightmare-inducing enemies in the entire Zelda franchise, and apparently, Nintendo knows exactly how much we fear this thing. Because if there's one boss that the remake refuses to make less terrifying, it's this horrifying creature!

Just like with the Iron Knuckle, your first encounter with Dead Hand happens while playing as Child Link. Veteran players already know what's coming as soon as they enter the room and spot those creepy hands emerging from the ground. And you can feel the tension building before it actually appears. Once it finally reveals itself, things get considerably worse.

Its updated design makes its face even more disturbing, and watching it attempt to bite Link with its enormous mouth is enough to make you question whether you accidentally launched a survival horror game instead of Ocarina of Time. I honestly don't know how Nintendo managed to make this thing even creepier, but I certainly won't be looking under my bed tonight.

Nintendo has expanded one of the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most heartbreaking side stories.

Fighting an invisible enemy is already challenging enough. Fighting an invisible enemy while standing on top of a giant bongo drum that it's constantly playing? Now that's a completely different story.

Bongo Bongo is easily one of the most creative boss encounters in Ocarina of Time, and its updated appearance takes the entire experience to another level. The idea of fighting this enormous, headless creature while trying to keep your balance on a drum is already wonderfully bizarre, but the atmosphere surrounding the encounter makes it even better.

The remake also makes some of its attacks noticeably faster, meaning you'll have even less time to react while trying to keep up with the rhythm of the fight. And since Bongo Bongo is literally drumming throughout the entire encounter, you can bet that things get pretty intense! It's such an unusual boss concept, and I love how the remake manages to preserve its original identity while making the entire battle feel even more chaotic.

Facing Dark Link is one of the most memorable moments in the original Ocarina of Time, and the remake manages to make this encounter just as special. As you progress through the Water Temple, you'll find yourself fighting Dark Link (accompanied by a rather creepy-looking Dark Navi, by the way), which ends up being an unforgettable battle.

The symbolism behind this encounter is already fantastic, since what better way to challenge the Hero of Time than by forcing him to face a darker version of himself? But the remake takes things even further by giving Dark Link a new move that might just be the coolest animation I've seen in the entire game.

Whenever you try to attack him with the tip of the Master Sword, he can actually dodge your strike by jumping onto the blade and standing on it – yes, he literally uses your own sword as a platform to avoid being hit, and it's ridiculously stylish! I also swear the controller gives you a little vibration when he pulls off this move, which makes the moment even more satisfying. Or maybe I'm imagining things because I'm still trying to process how cool it looks. Either way, Dark Link remains one of the best highlights of this remake.

I'll admit that Phantom Ganon has always been my favorite boss in the original Ocarina of Time, and a reason for that is the incredible atmosphere surrounding the Forest Temple. By the time you reach this dungeon, you've already seen what Ganondorf has done to Hyrule during his seven-year reign of terror, and there's a constant sense of dread surrounding his presence.

So, when you finally reach the boss room and see what appears to be Ganondorf himself, it's a pretty intimidating moment! Even if is a phantom version of him. What I love about it is that it uses a painting mechanic, where Phantom Ganon hides inside the painting and you must pay attention to spot him before he strikes you! Visually, it is a truly striking moment, and when he gets off the painting to face you off is amazing.

Also, the remake makes this encounter even more memorable by extending Ganondorf's dialogue after the battle. Once the boss is defeated, the real villain appears and calls him a useless puppet, warning that he knows Link’s intentions and won’t let him accomplish them so easily.

Twinrova just hits differently in the remake. The combination of their updated designs, new animations, and fully voiced cutscenes makes this battle feel considerably more special than it already was in the original. Gameplay-wise, the fight remains faithful to its original mechanics. You'll need to use the Mirror Shield to absorb the correct elemental attacks from Koume and Kotake before redirecting that energy toward the opposite witch. It's a clever mechanic that forces you to pay attention to both enemies while carefully timing your movements.

However, what really makes this encounter shine is how expressive the two witches have become! Their personalities come through much more clearly now, especially when you're managing to land a successful attack. Watching them react to your moves, get increasingly frustrated, and argue with each other is genuinely hilarious.

Things get considerably more serious once they fuse into Twinrova, turning the encounter into an even more intense battle involving both fire and ice. But the fun doesn't stop when the fight ends. The final interactions between the two witches are fantastic, and their newly voiced dialogue gives the entire sequence so much personality. Honestly, I could watch these two argue for hours.

There was no way I could finish this list without giving the final boss encounter the top spot. Facing Ganondorf and, eventually, Ganon is the culmination of everything you've experienced throughout Ocarina of Time, and the remake manages to make this already iconic confrontation even more impressive.

His updated animations, additional moves, and much more expressive character model make every moment feel considerably more dramatic. You can really feel that you're facing the main villain who has been threatening Hyrule throughout your entire adventure, rather than just another boss waiting at the end of a dungeon.

And then, just when you think the battle is over, Ganondorf transforms into Ganon, giving you one final confrontation against an enormous beast that looks terrifying in the remake's updated visuals. It's the perfect way to bring the adventure to its conclusion and also to deliver the best-looking sequences of the entire game. Now, if you'll excuse me, I think I need to replay the entire game again.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has only been out for a short while, and yet there are several mods that change major aspects of the game.

Built on Android Automotive OS, Hyundai’s new setup features a larger, tablet-style infotainment screen with apps, split-screen views, and more. It’s similar to using a smartphone with an easier-to-use, customizable layout.

Is the IONIQ 5 next in line? Hyundai aims to launch its first SDV as early as next year, and the IONIQ 5 appears to be a contender.

#4381. Gift Guide: The Absolute Best Gifts for Car Lovers

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Whether it’s the holidays, a birthday, or any occasion, we’ve got you covered with these editor-picked gift ideas for auto enthusiasts.

This article was updated with new products and information in November 2026.

If you’re here, chances are you or someone on your gift list is a self-proclaimed car lover. Simple, right? No, not so much. Car lovers consist of different personalities and interests, and finding the right gift for your favorite one can be tricky. To complicate things further, each car enthusiast has their own favorite ride or style, making it challenging to find a one-size-fits-all gift.

We scoured the interweb (and our own collections) for the best car-adjacent goodies and discovered some fantastic gifts sure to bring a smile to any auto enthusiast’s face. Whether you’re shopping for a birthday, graduation, or the holiday season, here are the best gifts for car lovers, as selected by the editors of Car and Driver.

The Model T needs no introduction, as it is perhaps the most influential vehicle of all time. Your favorite car lover will enjoy building this Lego-fied Tin Lizzie, complete with white rubber tires, a gold grille, and a fabric folding roof. You can even turn the crank to rotate the fan (no worries about arm-breaking kickback here!). At just over 1000 pieces, it hits that engaging sweet spot between too simple and overly complicated.

Or, if you’re looking for a Lego alternative, Mattel has sprung onto the scene with their Brick Shop builds, featuring an impressive catalogue of vehicular options. We tried out this RS2 kit, the Audi Quattro, and the 1990 Acura NSX, and were blown away by the quality. These aren’t knock-off buildable cars; they’re just as good, and their price points make them especially alluring.

Better yet, these building sets come with their own die-cast version of the car you just built. For a car lover, these are affordable yet impressive gifts for earning some nostalgic brownie points.

Forza Horizon 6 was the most popular racing game of the year thanks to its stunning setting in Japan, where you can explore with a wide array of vehicles. Xbox players have been enjoying it since launch, and the PlayStation version will be released at the end of January 2027. We’ve been thoroughly loving our playthrough—we think your giftee will too.

A glossy, 400-plus-page tour of 34 screen legends on two and four wheels. From Bond’s DB5 and Bullitt’s GT 390 to Thelma & Louise’s ’66 Thunderbird and the Dark Knight’s Tumbler, each chapter pairs knockout photography and illustrations with behind-the-scenes stories. Edited by Chad Oppenheim, Chris Nashawaty, and Matt Stone—with a foreword by Jay Leno and fresh voices, including Stephen King, Michael Bay, and Jeff Gordon—this is the coffee-table pit pass for anyone who judges movies by their chase scenes.

This is the dash cam for drivers who hate the look of dash cams. Roughly the size of a key fob, the Mini 3 hides neatly behind a rearview mirror and runs a “set it and forget it” loop without cluttering your view.

The big upgrade for this generation is a built-in polarizing filter, which significantly cuts down on the dashboard glare that often washes out footage in bright sunlight. Because it lacks a screen, you’ll need to rely on the Garmin Drive app to review clips or adjust settings, but the voice controls are responsive enough to save video of an incident without taking your hands off the wheel.

This is more than just a NASCAR driving experience—it’s your favorite car lover’s chance to drive a real NASCAR race car on the same track where legends like Dale Earnhardt and Jeff Gordon carved their names in history. They’ll feel the roar of 600 horsepower as they blaze down the 3800-foot straightaway, tackling the renowned 31-degree banked turns, and reaching top speeds of up to 160 mph. Whether you give them a quick eight-minute session or go for the full 48-minute marathon, this is a driving experience they’ll never forget.

If your favorite car lover is interested in new ways to avoid speeding tickets, consider gifting this top-of-the-line radar detector from Uniden. It was our top pick in our most recent radar detector test, boasting excellent results across the board for sniffing out Smokey.

For a more affordable option, try the Uniden R4w. It’s not as feature laden as its bigger brother, but the price is sure tough to beat.

We love vintage automotive shirts, and this one from Popfunk celebrates the iconic Civic in all its throwback glory. Featuring a cool blue background with a classic Civic font and the car star of the show, it's a must-have for any JDM fan.

The Marlin is Timex’s midcentury legend, and now it comes in a racing-inspired design. Racing stripes line the dial of this chronograph tachymeter, which features a 24-hour subdial decorated with checkered flags. Driven by an ultraprecise quartz movement, it includes a chronograph for tracking elapsed time and a tachymeter index along its outer minute track for measuring speed.

It retains classic Marlin features with a sturdy 40mm stainless steel case, domed acrylic crystal, retro-style applied indices, and a leather strap. We got our hands on the blue variant and vainly enjoy the countless compliments we receive on this watch.

A jump starter and a battery charger? Count us in. This handy device from industry stalwart Battery Tender is one of the handiest devices we’ve ever used—particularly on vehicles that are typically stored over the winter months, such as classic cars, motorcycles, and UTVs. This charger boasts up to 1200 amps of jump-starting power and 4 amps to help maintain your battery.

Any driveway mechanic will tell you that hand tools have a way of sprouting legs and making a run for it and that they’re usually successful in getting away. Refresh your favorite car tinkerer’s kit with this DeWALT Mechanic’s Tool Set. It comes with 172 pieces in a hard-shell blow-molded case with 72 tooth ratchets.

From the Lego Technic Ultimate Car Concept series: Your favorite car lover will be able to recreate the features of the Ferrari Daytona SP3 in classic red with chrome-painted rims. Features include steering, an eight-speed sequential gearbox with paddle shifter, a V-12 engine with moving pistons, and opening butterfly doors.

Created especially for adults, the completed 1:8 scale model will make a fantastic display piece for any auto enthusiast’s office or workspace.

Ranger Station creates some excellent scents, and we’ve thankfully gotten our hands on a few of their car air fresheners. With collaborations including Noah Kahan and Willie Nelson, these unique aromas are perfect for making your ride smell great.

This monstrous book, published by Taschen, is the ultimate collection of Ferrari lore and exploits, beautifully bound in Ferrari red. Chock full of gorgeous, full-page photos (including many previously unseen), documents, and sketches, this book connects the aura of Ferrari—perfect for the Ferrari fan in your life.

Most of us can say the first car we ever bought was a Hot Wheels, and this limited-print deluxe hardcover goes under the hood of the world’s number one toy brand, tracing its history and revealing the design process from first sketch to prototype to die-cast.

Legendary designer Larry Wood pens the foreword, and designers past and present talk shop about iconic builds such as the life-size Darth Vader Hot Wheels. There are incredible photos, drawings, and—make room in your garage—an exclusive special-edition Custom Camaro die-cast, honoring one of the Original 16 Hot Wheels cars. Display-worthy box included.

Corny? Depends on your POV, but at this price point, you can rationalize these interior LED lights as a gag gift. Thanks to a built-in mic, the colors and light speed adjust automatically to any music type. The app lets you access 16 million colors, a host of dynamic light effects, and an easy-to-use DIY mode. The strip lights boast a two-line design, which is ideal for the cockpit of any car, truck, or SUV.

Yep, it’s silly all right. But funnier than a Crown Royal bag. Plenty of colors are available.

Head-up displays are all the rage these days, and rightfully so. By displaying information closer to where your eyes are while driving, checking your speed becomes less of a distraction. But what if you want to see more information on your vehicle? This heads-up display shows coolant temperature, engine rpm, and more. It simply plugs into your OBD-II port and mounts on your dashboard.

We love BougeRV electric car coolers! These handy devices are real game-changers on road trips, car camping vacations, or even during your daily commute. They come in a variety of sizes for any traveler, and most are available in black or white. You can also check out the new Rocky line of overlanding-specific truck and Jeep coolers.

Want to see how many calories you can burn carving up mountain roads? Yes, that’s a thing—and the Polar Loop health band can tell you. The screenless design is ideal for driving (no distractions), and the live heart rate and sleep scoring provide great data to see how spirited driving benefits your health—something we’re very supportive of.

The best gift depends on how they enjoy cars. A model-building kit or automotive book suits a collector; a dash cam, jump starter, or battery maintainer is useful for a hands-on driver; and a racing game or track experience can make a memorable gift. This guide includes ideas across all of those interests.

A portable jump starter is a useful pick for someone who likes to be prepared for a dead battery. A dash cam can help record the road, while a battery maintainer is handy for vehicles that sit unused for long stretches, including classic cars and motorcycles.

Look for something they can enjoy outside the garage, such as a NASCAR driving experience, a beautifully illustrated book about car design, or a display-worthy model kit. A gift tied to a favorite marque, era, or racing series can make it feel more personal.

A small Lego set, a racing game, or interior LED lights can be fun gifts at a lower price point. Prices vary by retailer and can change, so check current listings before you buy.

#4380. A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

A promising new approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence. At the center of the breakthrough is a special class of materials known as multiferroics, which combine electrical and magnetic properties that can be controlled together using extremely small voltages.

These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology. However, a major obstacle has prevented their use in conventional computer chips. When multiferroics are made thin enough to fit inside these devices, they typically lose the electrical and magnetic behavior that makes them valuable. Scientists call this problem the "dead layer" effect.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces extremely thin films of bismuth ferrite, a widely studied multiferroic material, without sacrificing its essential properties. Even more remarkably, the process gives the material new magnetic characteristics that could make it especially useful for future electronics.

"We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer," said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. "We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want -- down to a few angstroms -- and it's still ferroelectric, and it's still magnetic."

The findings were published in the journal Nature Materials.

Why Multiferroics Could Transform Computer Chips

What makes multiferroics so attractive for computing is the unusual connection between their electrical and magnetic properties. Their atomic structure is made up of repeating units in which positive and negative charges are positioned on opposite sides, creating a property known as electrical polarization.

Applying a small voltage can reverse this polarization, effectively switching the positions of the positive and negative charges. This provides a potential way to store digital information as binary values (ones and zeros) using very little electricity.

Because the material's magnetic behavior is linked to its electrical polarization, the stored information can also be retrieved magnetically. This combination could enable computer memory and logic components that require significantly less energy than existing technologies.

The challenge has been making these materials small enough for practical devices. Modern computer chips require exceptionally thin layers, but multiferroics traditionally stop functioning properly when reduced to such dimensions.

Two separate effects cause this breakdown. First, the material's atomic structure becomes distorted, disrupting the arrangement and chemical environment necessary for its properties to function. Second, internal electric fields interfere with the material's polarization until it can no longer be maintained. Together, these effects destroy both its ferroelectric and magnetic behavior, creating the troublesome dead layer.

How Brown Engineers Eliminated the Dead Layer

To solve the problem, the Brown University team developed a new method for producing thin films of bismuth ferrite.

The researchers deposited the material onto a foundation made of dysprosium scandate, a compound derived from rare earth elements. This underlying material has a crystal structure with slightly smaller dimensions than bismuth ferrite, creating a mismatch between their atomic arrangements.

That mismatch places the bismuth ferrite under compression, helping preserve the atomic structure required for its electrical and magnetic properties to remain intact.

The team also incorporated a second metallic layer designed to counteract unwanted electric fields. By preventing those fields from disrupting the material's electrical polarization, the additional layer addresses the other major cause of the dead layer effect.

Together, these changes allow the bismuth ferrite film to retain its multiferroic properties even when reduced to just a few angstroms in thickness.

But the researchers discovered something else. Rather than simply preserving the material's original capabilities, their approach actually improved its magnetic behavior.

The engineered layers caused the bismuth ferrite to exhibit altermagnetism, an unusual form of magnetism that combines useful characteristics of two more familiar magnetic states: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

This discovery could be particularly important for developing faster and more compact computer components.

"Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out," Caretta said. "The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds -- they can be fast, densely integrated and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout."

In other words, altermagnets offer a potentially valuable combination of speed, compactness, and readable signals. These characteristics could help engineers build computer components that operate efficiently without the interference problems associated with conventional magnetic materials.

The ability to create this magnetic behavior in an exceptionally thin multiferroic film makes the discovery especially promising for future chip designs.

A New Path Toward Energy-Efficient AI Computing

As artificial intelligence continues to drive demand for computing power, developing hardware that consumes less electricity has become an increasingly important goal.

Caretta believes the new findings could help bring multiferroic materials closer to practical use in low-power memory and computing devices. Although the technology still needs further development before it can be incorporated into commercial chips, the research demonstrates that a long-standing materials limitation can be overcome.

It also shows that carefully engineering a material's atomic environment can do more than preserve its existing properties. Under the right conditions, it can produce useful behavior that was not present in the original material.

"We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials," Caretta said. "The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that's useful -- and sometimes even better than what nature gives us."

The research received funding from the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

#4378. Honda Just Teased a New Hybrid SUV Called the Avancier

The revived nameplate is expected to debut in Thailand next month as Honda prepares a major expansion of its hybrid lineup.

Honda is reviving the Avancier name for what looks like a new SUV, as first reported by Automotive News, suggesting the model could play a role in the automaker’s renewed push into hybrids.

Honda posted teaser images of an all-new Avancier on some of its global social-media channels, showing a sharply styled vehicle with slim taillights connected by a full-width light bar. The company has not released any specifications, but the teaser confirms that the Avancier will be one of the first models to use Honda’s new-generation hybrid technology.

See all results for used Honda for sale near 20191

The Avancier name has been used twice before. Honda originally sold it in Japan as a wagon from 1999 to 2003, then revived the name in 2016 for a larger, more upscale Chinese-spec crossover. The new version appears to be headed in a different direction than either, with reports pointing to a three-row SUV slotting above the CR-V, though none of those details have been confirmed by Honda.

Thai media reports say the new Avancier will make its world debut at the Thailand International Motor Expo on December 1.

More important than the nameplate may be what’s under the hood. Honda announced last month that it would call its next-generation hybrid system “Honda Hybrid,” with global launches beginning in 2027. The automaker says it plans to introduce 15 next-generation hybrid models worldwide by the end of fiscal 2029, with North America a primary focus.

Honda says the new hybrid system is designed to cost more than 30 percent less than the system introduced in the 2023 Accord while improving fuel economy by more than 10 percent. The system uses a redesigned engine and hybrid drive unit and can be paired with a newly developed electric all-wheel-drive system.

That strategy represents a big shift for Honda. Like many other automakers, Honda had been pushing aggressively toward EVs, but changing market conditions have prompted it to put more development resources into hybrids. Honda plans to make all of its North American auto plants capable of building hybrid vehicles and expects to launch larger hybrid models in the region beginning in 2029.

Whether the Avancier will come to the United States remains unclear. Honda has not announced U.S. availability, and the company has previously indicated that some next-generation hybrids will be tailored to specific markets. For now, the Avancier appears to be an early look at the new direction of Honda’s global hybrid.

#4377. Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

Tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The company confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a new production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

That’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:

If you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we announced a first investment of around € 3b in a new manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW

Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the new production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla plans to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company says it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”

It leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the new hall will be bigger than the original factory.

The building isn’t new. Tesla laid out a plan to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only said the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

Giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the new hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

The EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Rules can move in three years. The Commission has said it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

The Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU said no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

And the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

This is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

#4376. Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors

Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.
